title: Task-Adaptive Embedding Refinement via Test-time LLM Guidance
summary: We explore the effectiveness of an LLM-guided query refinement paradigm for extending the usability of embedding models to challenging zero-shot search and classification tasks. Our approach refines the embedding representation of a user query using feedback from a generative LLM on a small set of documents, enabling embeddings to adapt in real time to the target task. We conduct extensive experiments with state-of-the-art text embedding models across a diverse set of challenging search and classification benchmarks. Empirical results indicate that LLM-guided query refinement yields consistent gains across all models and datasets, with relative improvements of up to +25% in literature search, intent detection, key-point matching, and nuanced query-instruction following. The refined queries improve ranking quality and induce clearer binary separation across the corpus, enabling the embedding space to better reflect the nuanced, task-specific constraints of each ad-hoc user query. Importantly, this expands the range of practical settings in which embedding models can be effectively deployed, making them a compelling alternative when costly LLM pipelines are not viable at corpus-scale. We release our experimental code for reproducibility, at https://github.com/IBM/task-aware-embedding-refinement.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a method for refining text embedding representations using feedback from a generative LLM during test-time. Specifically, it leverages LLMs to improve the embedding of user queries based on a small set of documents, thereby adapting the embeddings to the specific task at hand. This is done by iteratively refining the query representation to better align with the specific nuances required for search and classification tasks. This adaptive querying allows the embedding space to dynamically respond to nuanced requirements, without requiring retraining of the embedding model.
data_sources: The abstract mentions experiments across a diverse set of challenging search and classification benchmarks. While it doesn't specify financial datasets directly in the abstract, the methodology can be applied to analyze financial news, earnings call transcripts, and analyst reports to generate better signals.
alpha_potential: This method can potentially improve the performance of text-based trading strategies. For example, by refining queries related to financial news or sentiment analysis, it could identify subtle signals indicating market movements or company performance. By adapting investor sentiment or risk perception in real time, it can inform dynamic portfolio allocation or high-frequency trading algorithms, leading to improved prediction accuracy and profitability by better capturing the signal in textual data. This could be applied to improve the understanding of earnings call transcripts or in the interpretation of analyst reports.

title: Predicting Decisions of AI Agents from Limited Interaction through Text-Tabular Modeling
summary: AI agents negotiate and transact in natural language with unfamiliar counterparts: a buyer bot facing an unknown seller, or a procurement assistant negotiating with a supplier. In such interactions, the counterpart's LLM, prompts, control logic, and rule-based fallbacks are hidden, while each decision can have monetary consequences. We ask whether an agent can predict an unfamiliar counterpart's next decision from a few interactions. To avoid real-world logging confounds, we study this problem in controlled bargaining and negotiation games, formulating it as target-adaptive text-tabular prediction: each decision point is a table row combining structured game state, offer history, and dialogue, while $K$ previous games of the same target agent, i.e., the counterpart being modeled, are provided in the prompt as labeled adaptation examples. Our model is built on a tabular foundation model that represents rows using game-state features and LLM-based text representations, and adds LLM-as-Observer as an additional representation: a small frozen LLM reads the decision-time state and dialogue; its answer is discarded, and its hidden state becomes a decision-oriented feature, making the LLM an encoder rather than a direct few-shot predictor. Training on 13 frontier-LLM agents and testing on 91 held-out scaffolded agents, the full model outperforms direct LLM-as-Predictor prompting and game+text features baselines. Within this tabular model, Observer features contribute beyond the other feature schemes: at $K=16$, they improve response-prediction AUC by about 4 points across both tasks and reduce bargaining offer-prediction error by 14%. These results show that formulating counterpart prediction as a target-adaptive text-tabular task enables effective adaptation, and that hidden LLM representations expose decision-relevant signals that direct prompting does not surface.
core_methodology: The paper proposes a target-adaptive text-tabular prediction model to predict the decisions of AI agents in negotiation games. It combines structured game-state features, offer history, and dialogue using a tabular foundation model augmented with LLM-based text representations. A key component is the 'LLM-as-Observer,' a small, frozen LLM used as an encoder to extract decision-oriented features from the game state and dialogue, effectively capturing hidden signals that direct prompting misses. The model is trained on data from multiple agents and tested on unseen agents in a scaffolded manner.
data_sources: The paper uses simulated bargaining and negotiation games as its data source. These games involve AI agents interacting with each other, generating structured game-state data, offer histories, and natural language dialogues.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in the ability to predict the behavior of other market participants (represented as AI agents) based on limited interaction history and textual communication. This could be applied to understanding the negotiation strategies of institutional investors, predicting the order execution behavior of algorithmic traders, or even identifying subtle biases in market sentiment as expressed through news articles or social media. By modeling the latent decision-making processes of other market actors, a trader could gain a strategic advantage in negotiation, order placement, and overall market timing.

title: ProfiliTable: Profiling-Driven Tabular Data Processing via Agentic Workflows
summary: Table processing-including cleaning, transformation, augmentation, and matching-is a foundational yet error-prone stage in real-world data pipelines. While recent LLM-based approaches show promise for automating such tasks, they often struggle in practice due to ambiguous instructions, complex task structures, and the lack of structured feedback, resulting in syntactically correct but semantically flawed code. To address these challenges, we propose ProfiliTable, an autonomous multi-agent framework centered on dynamic profiling, which constructs and iteratively refines a unified execution context through interactive exploration, knowledge-augmented synthesis, and feedback-driven refinement. ProfiliTable integrates (i) a Profiler that performs ReAct-style data exploration to build semantic understanding, (ii) a Generator that retrieves curated operators to synthesize task-aware code, and (iii) an Evaluator-Summarizer loop that injects execution scores and diagnostic insights to enable closed-loop refinement. Extensive experiments on a diverse benchmark covering 18 tabular task types demonstrate that ProfiliTable consistently outperforms strong baselines, particularly in complex multi-step scenarios. These results highlight the critical role of dynamic profiling in reliably translating ambiguous user intents into robust and governance-compliant table transformations.
core_methodology: The paper proposes ProfiliTable, an LLM-based autonomous multi-agent framework for robust and governance-compliant tabular data processing. It uses dynamic profiling for interactive data exploration, knowledge-augmented code synthesis using curated operators, and iterative feedback-driven refinement to address the challenge of ambiguous instructions and complex task structures in real-world data pipelines. The framework leverages a Profiler, a Generator, and an Evaluator-Summarizer loop, working in a ReAct-style manner for enhanced semantic understanding.
data_sources: While the abstract doesn't explicitly mention financial data, the techniques are applicable to cleaning, transforming, and augmenting financial datasets like fundamental data, alternative data (e.g., news sentiment), or economic indicators which can be considered tabular data sources.
alpha_potential: The ability to reliably clean, transform, and augment complex, multi-source financial datasets has high alpha potential. Improved data quality can lead to more accurate model inputs, reducing noise and bias in trading signals. Specifically, more effectively processing unstructured or semi-structured fundamental data, or integrating messy alternative datasets with market data, could unveil new predictive features for factor models or statistical arbitrage strategies. Furthermore, the governance-compliant aspect is valuable in regulated financial environments.

title: Hypernetworks for Dynamic Feature Selection
summary: Dynamic feature selection (DFS) is a machine learning framework in which features are acquired sequentially for individual samples under budget constraints. The exponential growth in the number of possible feature acquisition paths forces a DFS model to balance fitting specific scenarios against maintaining general performance, even when the feature space is moderate in size. In this paper, we study the structural limitations of existing DFS approaches to achieve an optimal solution. Then, we propose \textsc{Hyper-DFS}, a hypernetwork-based DFS approach that generates feature subset-specific classifier parameters on demand. We show that the use of hypernetworks compared to mask-embedding methods results in a smaller structural complexity bound. We also use a Set Transformer encoding to create a smooth conditioning space for the hypernetwork, so that functionally similar tasks are also geometrically close. In our benchmarks, \textsc{Hyper-DFS} outperforms all state-of-the-art approaches on synthetic and real-life tabular data. It is also competitive or superior across all image datasets tested, and shows substantially stronger zero-shot generalisation to feature subsets never seen during training than existing DFS approaches.
core_methodology: The paper proposes Hyper-DFS, a dynamic feature selection method based on hypernetworks. It dynamically selects features based on individual samples and budget constraints. The hypernetwork generates feature subset-specific classifier parameters, and a Set Transformer encoding is used to create a smooth conditioning space. This allows for better generalization and handling of various feature subsets.
data_sources: The paper benchmarks the approach on synthetic data, real-life tabular data, and image datasets. For financial applications, this implies the need for structured, tabular data, possibly incorporating various market indicators or alternative data sources.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in the ability to dynamically select the most relevant features for a given market condition or asset, potentially improving prediction accuracy and reducing overfitting. For example, in a momentum strategy, it can dynamically select features related to volume, price changes, volatility, or macroeconomic variables that are most predictive during specific periods or regimes, leading to improved risk-adjusted returns. By focusing on the most influential indicators at any given time and minimizing model complexity, Hyper-DFS offers an approach to potentially capture transient market opportunities more accurately.

title: RED-2400: A Public Benchmark of Algorithmically-Rejected Trading Events with Outcome Labels
summary: RED-2400 is a public benchmark of algorithmically-rejected trading events from a live Solana decentralized-exchange filter stack. I logged the data continuously between 2026-04-10 and 2026-05-02. The benchmark contains 6,659 rejection events linked to 169,122 post-rejection price and liquidity observations and 1,836 graveyard-tracker snapshots. Outcome labels follow the five-tier classification of Kamat (2026c): saved (windowed), saved (early-death), missed, flat, and unclassifiable. Thresholds use the trough-to-reference and peak-to-reference price ratios within a 24-hour window. Most filter-design datasets cover the accept side only. That gap leaves reject-side outcomes unmeasured and biases filter validation. RED-2400 lets researchers replicate filter-precision claims directly. RED-2400 is the first window in a planned dataset series; subsequent windows will extend the time horizon and enable regime-stratified analysis.
core_methodology: The paper presents a benchmark dataset (RED-2400) of algorithmically-rejected trading events on a Solana DEX. It provides outcome labels based on price movements after the rejection (saved, missed, etc.) using trough-to-reference and peak-to-reference price ratios. The dataset is designed to help improve the precision of trading filters and analyze the impact of rejecting trades.
data_sources: Live Solana decentralized exchange (DEX) data, specifically algorithmically-rejected trading events and subsequent price/liquidity observations.
alpha_potential: The dataset allows researchers to analyze the performance of existing filters and discover new features and models to predict whether rejecting a trade will lead to a favorable outcome (e.g., avoiding a loss). This information can be used to build more sophisticated filter logic, leading to improved risk management and potentially higher profitability in algorithmic trading strategies on DEXs. Furthermore, analyzing the reasons for rejection can identify inefficiencies, or 'blind spots' in current algorithmic execution setups.

summary_cn: RED-2400 是一个 Solona DEX 上算法拒绝交易事件的基准数据集。通过分析拒绝交易后的价格表现，可以优化交易过滤器，提高算法交易的风控能力和潜在盈利。 该数据集对提升在去中心化交易所的算法交易策略具有重要意义, 通过分析拒绝原因，可以识别当前算法执行设置中的低效或“盲点”。

title: Martingale-Consistent Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is often deployed under changing information, such as shorter histories, missing features, or partially observed images. In these settings, predictions from coarse and refined views should be coherent: before refinement, the coarse-view prediction should match the average prediction expected after refinement. Martingales formalize this coherence principle, but standard SSL objectives do not enforce it. Unlike invariance objectives that pull views together, martingale consistency constrains only the expected refined prediction, allowing predictions to update as information is revealed while preventing systematic drift. We introduce a martingale-consistent SSL framework that closes this gap, with practical prediction- and latent-space variants and an unbiased two-sample Monte Carlo estimator based on stochastic refinement. We evaluate the approach on synthetic and real time-series, tabular, and image benchmarks under partial-observation regimes, in both semi-self-supervised and fully label-free settings. Across these experiments, our framework improves robustness and calibration under partial observation, yielding more stable representations as information is revealed.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a martingale-consistent self-supervised learning (SSL) framework to improve robustness and calibration of models under partial observation. It ensures that predictions from different 'views' of the data (coarse and refined) are coherent in a martingale sense, preventing systematic drift as more information is revealed. This is achieved through prediction- and latent-space variants and an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator.
data_sources: The paper evaluates the framework on synthetic and real time-series, tabular, and image benchmarks. Specific financial data sources aren't explicitly mentioned but can be applied to stock prices, order book data, macro economic data, or alternative data sets.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in improving the stability and consistency of predictions when using incomplete or evolving data.  In trading, data is frequently missing or subject to revisions (e.g., earnings estimates, economic indicators, order flow). By enforcing martingale consistency, predictions can become more robust to noisy, incomplete, or evolving information streams, leading to better risk management and potentially improved signal extraction, especially in high-frequency trading where rapid updates and partial observability are common. The framework can be helpful in modeling market microstructure dynamics and capturing signals that would otherwise be missed due to data imperfections.

summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种鞅一致性自监督学习框架，提高了模型在部分观测下的鲁棒性和校准。该方法确保了不同数据'视图'（粗略和精细）的预测在鞅意义上是一致的，防止了随着信息揭示而产生的系统性漂移。这可以应用于股票价格、订单簿数据等金融时间序列，提高模型在不完整或不断变化的数据下的预测稳定性，从而改进风险管理并提取更优信号。

title: GeomHerd: A Forward-looking Herding Quantification via Ricci Flow Geometry on Agent Interactive Simulations
summary: Herding -- where agents align their behaviors and act collectively -- is a central driver of market fragility and systemic risk. Existing approaches to quantify herding rely on price-correlation statistics, which inherently lag because they only detect coordination after it has already moved realised returns. We propose GeomHerd, a forward-looking geometric framework that bypasses this observability lag by quantifying coordination directly on upstream agent-interaction graphs. To generate these graphs, we treat a heterogeneous LLM-driven multi-agent simulator -- each financial trader instantiated by a persona-conditioned LLM call -- as a forecastable world, and evaluate the geometric pipeline on the Cividino--Sornette continuous-spin agent-based substrate as our headline financial testbed. By tracking the discrete Ollivier--Ricci curvature of these action graphs, GeomHerd captures the structural topology of emerging coordination. Theoretically, we establish a mean-field bridge mapping our graph-theoretic metric to CSAD, the classical macroscopic herding statistic, linking GeomHerd to downstream price-dispersion measurement. Empirically, GeomHerd anticipates herding long before aggregate market baselines: on the continuous-spin substrate, our primary detector fires a median of 272 steps before order-parameter onset; a contagion detector ($β_{-}$) recalls 65% of critical trajectories 318 steps early; and on co-firing trajectories the agent-graph signal precedes price-correlation-graph baselines by 40 steps. As a complementary indicator, the effective vocabulary of agent actions contracts during cascades. The geometric signature transfers out-of-domain to the Vicsek self-driven-particle model, and a curvature-conditioned forecasting head reduces cascade-window log-return MAE over detector-conditioned and price-only baselines.
core_methodology: The paper introduces GeomHerd, a novel forward-looking herding quantification framework. It uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to simulate financial traders and their interactions, creating agent-interaction graphs. The discrete Ollivier-Ricci curvature of these graphs is then tracked to capture the structural topology of emerging coordination, providing an early warning signal for herding behavior compared to traditional price-correlation methods.
data_sources: The primary testbed is the Cividino-Sornette continuous-spin agent-based model. The paper also mentions the Vicsek self-driven-particle model for out-of-domain transfer.
alpha_potential: The key alpha potential lies in anticipating herding behavior before it manifests in price movements. By detecting coordination among simulated traders through the agent-interaction graph, the framework aims to provide an early signal for identifying potential market trends, and thus capitalize on price movements before they are fully reflected in traditional herding metrics. The early detection of critical trajectories in contagion events also offers an opportunity to profit from market reactions.

title: Efficient and provably convergent end-to-end training of deep neural networks with linear constraints
summary: Training a deep neural network with the outputs of selected layers satisfying linear constraints is required in many contemporary data-driven applications. While this can be achieved by incorporating projection layers into the neural network, its end-to-end training remains challenging due to the lack of rigorous theory and efficient algorithms for backpropagation. A key difficulty in developing the theory and efficient algorithms for backpropagation arose from the nonsmoothness of the solution mapping of the projection layer. To address this bottleneck, we introduce an efficiently computable HS-Jacobian to the projection layer. Importantly, we prove that the HS-Jacobian is a conservative mapping for the projection operator onto the polyhedral set, enabling its seamless integration into the nonsmooth automatic differentiation framework for backpropagation. Therefore, many efficient algorithms, such as Adam, can be applied for end-to-end training of deep neural networks with linear constraints. Particularly, we establish convergence guarantees of the HS-Jacobian based Adam algorithm for training linearly constrained deep neural networks. Extensive experiment results on several important applications, including finance, computer vision, and network architecture design, demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to other existing popular methods.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a novel HS-Jacobian for projection layers in deep neural networks, enabling efficient and provably convergent end-to-end training with linear constraints. This improved backpropagation allows for more stable and reliable training of constrained neural networks, particularly addressing the challenges of non-smoothness inherent in projection operators onto polyhedral sets. The method integrates seamlessly with existing optimization algorithms like Adam.
data_sources: The paper mentions applications in finance, computer vision, and network architecture design. Specific financial datasets are not identified in the abstract, but one would expect time-series data, order-book data, or other financial data depending on the experiment.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential comes from the ability to incorporate linear constraints into deep learning models used for trading. This could be applied to portfolio optimization (e.g., budget constraints, sector allocation constraints, risk limits), algorithmic trading strategy parameter optimization (e.g., constraints on bet sizing, risk exposure constraints based on VaR limits), or arbitrage strategies by enforcing constraints that directly represent arbitrage conditions. By ensuring constraints are met during the backpropagation and optimization process, the resulting trading strategies are more likely to adhere to rules and regulations and maintain stability in volatile market conditions. It could also be applied to momentum strategies to constrain the weights based on market capitalization or other criteria.
title_cn: 具有线性约束的深度神经网络的高效且可证明收敛的端到端训练
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种新的HS-Jacobian方法，能够高效地训练具有线性约束的深度神经网络。该方法通过改进反向传播算法，克服了传统方法中由于投影层引起的非光滑性问题，使得模型训练更加稳定可靠。此方法可应用于投资组合优化、算法交易策略参数优化和套利策略，通过在训练过程中实施约束，确保交易策略符合规则，并在动荡的市场条件下保持稳定。

title: Adaptive Calibration in Non-Stationary Environments
summary: Making calibrated online predictions is a central challenge in modern AI systems. Much of the existing literature focuses on fully adversarial environments where outcomes may be arbitrary, leading to conservative algorithms that can perform suboptimally in more benign settings, such as when outcomes are nearly stationary. This gap raises a natural question: can we design online prediction algorithms whose calibration error automatically adapts to the degree of non-stationarity in the environment, smoothly interpolating between i.i.d. and adversarial regimes? We answer this question in the affirmative and develop a suite of algorithms that achieve adaptive calibration guarantees under multiple calibration measures. Specifically, with $T$ being the number of rounds and $C\in[0,T]$ being an unknown non-stationary measure defined as the minimal $\ell_1$ deviation of the mean outcomes, our algorithms attain $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}+(TC)^{\frac{1}{3}})$ for $\ell_1$ calibration error and $\widetilde{O}((1+C)^{\frac{1}{3}})$ for both $\ell_2$ and pseudo KL calibration error. These bounds match the optimal rates in the stationary case ($C=0$) and recover known guarantees in the fully adversarial regime ($C=T$). Our approach builds on and extends prior work [Hu et al., 2026, Luo et al., 2025], introducing an epoch-based scheduling together with a novel non-uniform partition of the prediction space that allocates finer resolution near the underlying ground truth.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a suite of online prediction algorithms that adaptively calibrate to the degree of non-stationarity in the environment. It uses an epoch-based scheduling and a non-uniform partition of the prediction space to achieve optimal calibration error rates. The key innovation lies in dynamically adjusting the calibration strategy based on the estimated level of non-stationarity (measured by the minimal l1 deviation of mean outcomes, C). The algorithms achieve $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}+(TC)^{\frac{1}{3}})$ for $\ell_1$ calibration error and $\widetilde{O}((1+C)^{\frac{1}{3}})$ for both $\ell_2$ and pseudo KL calibration error, which are optimal in stationary environments and recover known guarantees in adversarial regimes. This involves sophisticated online learning techniques focused on calibration.
data_sources: The paper is theoretical and does not explicitly specify data sources. However, its adaptive calibration framework can be applied to any time series data where accurate probability calibration is crucial for decision-making. This includes price movements, order book data, sentiment scores, and macroeconomic indicators.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential comes from improved risk management and more accurate predictions in non-stationary market conditions. By adapting to changing market dynamics, the algorithms can reduce prediction errors and generate more reliable probability estimates. This can be particularly valuable for volatility forecasting, hedging strategies, and dynamic position sizing. The improved calibration can help avoid overconfidence or underconfidence in predictions, leading to better-informed trading decisions and enhanced profitability. By better calibrating predictions about regime changes, it could lead to improved trading system performance across cycles. In particular, well-calibrated probabilities of extreme events (tail risks) would provide strong tools for hedging extreme market moves.

summary_cn: 该论文提出了一套在线预测算法，能够自适应地校准非平稳环境中的预测。该算法通过epoch调度和非均匀预测空间划分，实现了最优的校准误差率。其核心在于根据非平稳程度动态调整校准策略，从而在不同市场状态下提供更准确的概率预测，进而改善风险管理和动态头寸调整，提高交易决策的盈利能力。

title: Generative Diffusion Prior Distillation for Long-Context Knowledge Transfer
summary: While traditional time-series classifiers assume full sequences at inference, practical constraints (latency and cost) often limit inputs to partial prefixes. The absence of class-discriminative patterns in partial data can significantly hinder a classifier's ability to generalize. This work uses knowledge distillation (KD) to equip partial time series classifiers with the generalization ability of their full-sequence counterparts. In KD, high-capacity teacher transfers supervision to aid student learning on the target task. Matching with teacher features has shown promise in closing the generalization gap due to limited parameter capacity. However, when the generalization gap arises from training-data differences (full versus partial), the teacher's full-context features can be an overwhelming target signal for the student's short-context features. To provide progressive, diverse, and collective teacher supervision, we propose Generative Diffusion Prior Distillation (GDPD), a novel KD framework that treats short-context student features as degraded observations of the target full-context features. Inspired by the iterative restoration capability of diffusion models, we learn a diffusion-based generative prior over teacher features. Leveraging this prior, we posterior-sample target teacher representations that could best explain the missing long-range information in the student features and optimize the student features to be minimally degraded relative to these targets. GDPD provides each student feature with a distribution of task-relevant long-context knowledge, which benefits learning on the partial classification task. Extensive experiments across earliness settings, datasets, and architectures demonstrate GDPD's effectiveness for full-to-partial distillation.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Generative Diffusion Prior Distillation (GDPD), a knowledge distillation framework using diffusion models to transfer knowledge from full-context time series classifiers (teachers) to partial-context classifiers (students). It addresses the challenge of limited context in time-series classification by training a generative prior over teacher features using a diffusion model. This prior allows sampling target teacher representations that explain missing long-range information in student features, effectively providing progressive and diverse supervision.
data_sources: The paper reports experiments across various datasets. While not explicitly financial datasets in the abstract, the methodology explicitly deals with time series data, making it potentially applicable to various types of financial data.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in the ability to improve the performance of classifiers that operate on partial or incomplete time series data. In trading, this could be used to make predictions based on incomplete market data (e.g., intraday data before market close) by leveraging a model pre-trained on full-day data. This could be useful for high-frequency trading or intraday momentum strategies, especially during volatile periods when the initial part of the day might be highly informative.
title_cn: 生成扩散先验蒸馏用于长程上下文知识迁移

title: MaskTab: Scalable Masked Tabular Pretraining with Scaling Laws and Distillation for Industrial Classification
summary: Tabular data forms the backbone of high-stakes decision systems in finance, healthcare, and beyond. Yet industrial tabular datasets are inherently difficult: high-dimensional, riddled with missing entries, and rarely labeled at scale. While foundation models have revolutionized vision and language, tabular learning still leans on handcrafted features and lacks a general self-supervised framework. We present MaskTab, a unified pre-training framework designed specifically for industrial-scale tabular data. MaskTab encodes missing values via dedicated learnable tokens, enabling the model to distinguish structural absence from random dropout. It jointly optimizes a hybrid supervised pre-training scheme--utilizing a twin-path architecture to reconcile masked reconstruction with task-specific supervision--and an MoE-augmented loss that adaptively routes features through specialized subnetworks. On industrial-scale benchmarks, it achieves +5.04% AUC and +8.28% KS over prior art under rigorous scaling. Moreover, its representations distill effectively into lightweight models, yielding +2.55% AUC and +4.85% KS under strict latency and interpretability constraints, while improving robustness to distribution shifts. Our work demonstrates that tabular data admits a foundation-model treatment--when its structural idiosyncrasies are respected.
core_methodology: MaskTab is a pre-training framework for tabular data using masked reconstruction, task-specific supervision with a twin-path architecture, and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) augmented loss. It handles missing values via dedicated learnable tokens. The pre-trained representations can be distilled into lightweight models.
data_sources: The paper focuses on industrial-scale tabular datasets, which can be interpreted as including financial datasets (e.g., credit risk assessment, fraud detection, loan default prediction) with high dimensionality, missing values, and limited labels. It does not explicitly specify market data
alpha_potential: The key alpha potential lies in creating robust and scalable features for predictive models. By pre-training on large, unlabeled datasets, MaskTab can learn representations of market regimes and cross-sectional relationships. These representations can then be fine-tuned for specific trading tasks, such as predicting stock returns, volatility, or order book dynamics. The ability to handle missing data and distribution shifts (e.g., due to economic events or market microstructure changes) provides a valuable edge. Furthermore, distillation into lightweight models enables efficient deployment in low-latency trading environments.

title: Beyond Similarity: Temporal Operator Attention for Time Series Analysis
summary: A persistent paradox in time-series forecasting is that structurally simple MLP and linear models often outperform high-capacity Transformers. We argue that this gap arises from a mismatch in the sequence-modeling primitive: while many time-series dynamics are governed by global temporal operators (e.g., filtering and harmonic structure), standard attention forms each output as a convex combination of inputs. This restricts its ability to represent signed and oscillatory transformations that are fundamental to temporal signal processing. We formalize this limitation as a simplex-constrained mixing bottleneck in softmax attention, which becomes especially restrictive for operator-driven time-series tasks. To address this, we propose $\textbf{Temporal Operator Attention (TOA)}$, a framework that augments attention with explicit, learnable sequence-space operators, enabling direct signed mixing across time while preserving input-dependent adaptivity. To make dense $N \times N$ operators practical, we introduce Stochastic Operator Regularization, a high-variance dropout mechanism that stabilizes training and prevents trivial memorization. Across forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification benchmarks, TOA consistently improves performance when integrated into standard backbones such as PatchTST and iTransformer, with particularly strong gains in reconstruction-heavy tasks. These results suggest that explicit operator learning is a key ingredient for effective time-series modeling.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Temporal Operator Attention (TOA), which augments standard attention mechanisms with learnable sequence-space operators to enable signed mixing across time. This addresses limitations of standard attention in representing oscillatory and filtering transformations common in time series. It uses Stochastic Operator Regularization (a high-variance dropout) to stabilize training and prevent overfitting. The method is integrated into PatchTST and iTransformer backbones.
data_sources: The abstract mentions forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification benchmarks, implying standard time-series datasets were used, potentially including financial time series data. Further investigation would be required to confirm specific datasets used for evaluation in the financial domain.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in improved modeling of temporal dependencies and oscillatory patterns in financial time series. This could lead to better forecasts of asset prices, improved anomaly detection (e.g., identifying flash crashes or fraudulent activity), and more accurate classification of market regimes. The ability to model signed transformations directly may be particularly helpful in capturing mean-reversion effects or detecting changes in correlations.

title: Latent Chain-of-Thought Improves Structured-Data Transformers
summary: Chain-of-thought and more broadly test-time compute are known to augment the expressive capabilities of language models and have led to major innovations in reasoning. Motivated by this success, this paper explores latent chain-of-thought as well as the impact of depth and looping for time-series and tabular data. We propose a recurrent scheme in which a structured-data transformer, after an initial forward pass, compresses its query-position hidden states into feedback tokens that are appended to the input and processed again, allowing multiple rounds of latent computation before prediction. We compare CoT models against a same-depth no-CoT baseline, a deeper baseline matched to the CoT model in effective depth, and a looped transformer with weight-tied recurrence but no additional chain-of-thought tokens. Across 36 datasets in time-series forecasting and tabular prediction, latent chain-of-thought improves over the baseline on 8/9 time-series datasets (+10.99\% average gain) and 22/27 tabular datasets (+5.31\% average gain). Across both settings, the CoT models perform the best on average. These results demonstrate that chain-of-thought is a useful axis for scaling test-time compute for structured data.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a 'latent chain-of-thought' (CoT) mechanism for structured-data transformers. This involves recurrently processing input data by compressing query-position hidden states into feedback tokens that are appended to the input for subsequent processing rounds. The goal is to enhance the model's ability to reason and extract complex temporal and relational patterns from time-series and tabular data. The approach is compared against baselines including non-CoT, deeper and looped transformer architectures.
data_sources: The study uses 36 datasets spanning time-series forecasting and tabular prediction tasks. While the specific datasets aren't detailed in the abstract, they likely include standard benchmark datasets used in these areas.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential stems from the enhanced reasoning capabilities of the latent CoT mechanism. In financial time series, this could translate to better identification of subtle trends, regime changes, and inter-market dependencies that are missed by standard models. A model with better reasoning about market microstructure and sentiment shifts could potentially lead to improved prediction accuracy for high-frequency trading, algorithmic execution, and portfolio construction strategies.

title: Model-based Bootstrap of Controlled Markov Chains
summary: We propose and analyze a model-based bootstrap for transition kernels in finite controlled Markov chains (CMCs) with possibly nonstationary or history-dependent control policies, a setting that arises naturally in offline reinforcement learning (RL) when the behavior policy generating the data is unknown. We establish distributional consistency of the bootstrap transition estimator in both a single long-chain regime and the episodic offline RL regime. The key technical tools are a novel bootstrap law of large numbers (LLN) for the visitation counts and a novel use of the martingale central limit theorem (CLT) for the bootstrap transition increments. We extend bootstrap distributional consistency to the downstream targets of offline policy evaluation (OPE) and optimal policy recovery (OPR) via the delta method by verifying Hadamard differentiability of the Bellman operators, yielding asymptotically valid confidence intervals for value and $Q$-functions. Experiments on the RiverSwim problem show that the proposed bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs), especially the percentile CIs, outperform the episodic bootstrap and plug-in CLT CIs, and are often close to nominal ($50\%$, $90\%$, $95\%$) coverage, while the baselines are poorly calibrated at small sample sizes and short episode lengths.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a model-based bootstrap method for transition kernels in finite controlled Markov chains (CMCs), particularly useful in offline reinforcement learning (RL) where the behavior policy is unknown. It focuses on estimating transition probabilities and downstream targets like value and Q-functions using bootstrap resampling. The core idea revolves around developing confidence intervals for offline policy evaluation (OPE) and optimal policy recovery (OPR) using a novel bootstrap law of large numbers (LLN) and martingale central limit theorem (CLT). Hadamard differentiability is used to extend consistency through the delta method.
data_sources: The experiments are conducted on the RiverSwim problem, which can be considered a stylized environment. For real-world finance applications, historical market data across various asset classes and timeframes, and potentially order book data, can be used to represent Markov chains of market states.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in creating more robust and reliable estimates of policy values and Q-functions in offline reinforcement learning for algorithmic trading strategies. Accurately estimating these values can lead to better policy optimization, and thus to better trading decisions. The method could improve risk management via better quantification of the uncertainty of estimated performance and thus better control over parameter selection. For example, one could use this to estimate the value of executing specific order types at high frequency, where data generating process is subject to change.

title: Detecting overfitting in Neural Networks during long-horizon grokking using Random Matrix Theory
summary: Training Neural Networks (NNs) without overfitting is difficult; detecting that overfitting is difficult as well. We present a novel Random Matrix Theory method that detects the onset of overfitting in deep learning models without access to train or test data. For each model layer, we randomize each weight matrix element-wise, $\mathbf{W} \to \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{rand}}$, fit the randomized empirical spectral distribution with a Marchenko-Pastur distribution, and identify large outliers that violate self-averaging. We call these outliers Correlation Traps. During the onset of overfitting, which we call the "anti-grokking" phase in long-horizon grokking, Correlation Traps form and grow in number and scale as test accuracy decreases while train accuracy remains high. Traps may be benign or may harm generalization; we provide an empirical approach to distinguish between them by passing random data through the trained model and evaluating the JS divergence of output logits. Our findings show that anti-grokking is an additional grokking phase with high train accuracy and decreasing test accuracy, structurally distinct from pre-grokking through its Correlation Traps. More broadly, we find that some foundation-scale LLMs exhibit the same Correlation Traps, indicating potentially harmful overfitting.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a Random Matrix Theory (RMT) based method to detect overfitting in neural networks. It randomizes weight matrices, fits the randomized empirical spectral distribution with a Marchenko-Pastur distribution, and identifies 'Correlation Traps' as outliers that violate self-averaging. These Correlation Traps indicate the onset of overfitting.
data_sources: The methodology does not explicitly rely on particular data sources, however, implicitly it utilizes data used to train the underlying neural network. The paper suggests an approach to use 'random data' passed through the trained model as a way to evaluate the JS divergence of output logits for trap evaluation. This implies that real market data, simulated data, or other types of random data could potentially be used.
alpha_potential: The ability to detect overfitting *without* access to train or test data is valuable. If this method can be applied to neural networks used in trading strategies, especially those trained on large datasets and prone to overfitting (e.g., models predicting price movements), it could improve the robustness and generalization ability of the trading strategy. By monitoring for Correlation Traps and mitigating overfitting, traders could potentially prevent performance degradation and enhance profitability.

title: Events as Triggers for Behavioral Diversity in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Effective multi-agent cooperation requires agents to adopt diverse behaviors as task conditions evolve-and to do so at the right moment. Yet, current Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) frameworks that facilitate this diversity are still limited by the fact that they bind fixed behaviors to fixed agent identities. Consequently, they are ill-equipped for tasks where agents need to take on different roles at very specific moments in time. We argue that, to define these behavioral transitions, the missing ingredient is events. Events are changes in the state of the system that induce qualitative changes in the task. Based on this view, we introduce a framework that decouples agent identity from behavior, capturing a continuous manifold from which agents instantiate their behaviors in response to events. This framework is based on two elements. First, to build an expressive behavior manifold, we introduce Neural Manifold Diversity (NMD), a formal distance metric that remains well-defined when behaviors are transient and agent-agnostic. Second, we use an event-based hypernetwork that generates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules over a shared team policy, enabling on-the-fly agent-policy reconfiguration in response to events. We prove that this construction ensures that diversity does not interfere with reward maximization by design. Empirical results demonstrate that our framework outperforms established baselines across benchmarks while exhibiting zero-shot generalization, and being the only method that solves tasks requiring sequential behavior reassignment.
core_methodology: The paper introduces a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework called Neural Manifold Diversity (NMD) coupled with an event-based hypernetwork using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to enable agents to dynamically switch roles based on environmental events. This aims to create adaptive and diverse agent behaviors for cooperative tasks.
data_sources: The abstract does not explicitly mention specific data sources. The paper focuses on the framework itself, implying that it can be applied to various environments that can be modeled within a MARL setting. Real-world financial market data (e.g., order book, news sentiment, macroeconomic indicators) could potentially be inputs to the agent's environment.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in the framework's ability to adapt to changing market conditions. By training agents to react to 'events' (defined changes in market state), the model could, in theory, capture non-stationary market dynamics better than traditional RL approaches. For example, an event could be a sudden change in volatility, interest rate announcements, or a news event that significantly shifts market sentiment. The model could then reconfigure its agent policies on the fly to take advantage of temporary inefficiencies or arbitrage opportunities created by these events.

title: Trust the Batch, On- or Off-Policy: Adaptive Policy Optimization for RL Post-Training
summary: Reinforcement learning is structurally harder than supervised learning because the policy changes the data distribution it learns from. The resulting fragility is especially visible in large-model training, where the training and rollout systems differ in numerical precision, sampling, and other implementation details. Existing methods manage this fragility by adding hyper-parameters to the training objective, which makes the algorithm more sensitive to its configuration and requires retuning whenever the task, model scale, or distribution mismatch changes. This fragility traces to two concerns that current objectives entangle through hyper-parameters set before training begins: a trust-region concern, that updates should not move the policy too far from its current value, and an off-policy concern, that data from older or different behavior policies should influence the update only to the extent that it remains reliable. Neither concern is a constant to set in advance, and their severity is reflected in the policy-ratio distribution of the current batch. We present a simple yet effective batch-adaptive objective that replaces fixed clipping with the normalized effective sample size of the policy ratios. The same statistic caps the score-function weight and sets the strength of an off-policy regularizer, so the update stays close to the usual on-policy score-function update when ratios are nearly uniform, and tightens automatically when stale or mismatched data cause ratio concentration, while retaining a nonzero learning signal on high-ratio tokens. Experiments across a wide range of settings show that our method matches or exceeds tuned baselines, introducing no new objective hyper-parameters and removing several existing ones. The code is available at https://github.com/FeynRL-project/FeynRL.
core_methodology: This paper introduces a batch-adaptive objective for reinforcement learning (RL) post-training that dynamically adjusts trust-region and off-policy constraints based on the policy-ratio distribution of the current batch. It replaces fixed clipping with the normalized effective sample size of the policy ratios. The approach focuses on improving the stability and sample efficiency of RL algorithms when deployed in settings where there are differences between the training and deployment environments.
data_sources: The paper doesn't specify direct market data usage in the abstract, but it is implied that the 'environments' where the method is tested might include simulations of real-world environments. It is crucial to understand the environments in which the method was applied in the full paper.
alpha_potential: The potential lies in more robust and adaptive policy execution in markets. If an RL agent is trained using historical data or a simulation environment, its performance can degrade rapidly when deployed to live trading conditions due to distribution mismatch and other real-world factors. A method that dynamically adjusts policy constraints could improve the agent's robustness and reduce the need for frequent retraining. This, in turn, minimizes losses during transition periods or when strategies are temporarily impaired, resulting in a more consistent profit generation.

title: Discrete Flow Matching for Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
summary: Many reinforcement learning (RL) tasks have discrete action spaces, but most generative policy methods based on diffusion and flow matching are designed for continuous control. Meanwhile, generative policies usually rely heavily on offline datasets and offline-to-online RL is itself challenging, as the policy must improve from new interaction without losing useful behavior learned from static data. To address those challenges, we introduce DRIFT, an online fine-tuning method that updates an offline pretrained continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) policy with an advantage-weighted discrete flow matching loss. To preserve useful pretrained knowledge, we add a path-space penalty that regularizes the full CTMC trajectory distribution, rather than only the final action distribution. For large discrete action spaces, we introduce a candidate-set approximation that updates the actor over a small subset of actions sampled from reference-policy rollouts and uniform exploration. Our theoretical analysis shows that the candidate-set error is controlled by missing target probability mass, and the induced CTMC generator error decreases as the candidate set covers more high-probability actions. Experiments on prevailing discrete action RL task show that our method provides stable offline-to-online improvement across all tasks, achieving the highest average score on Jericho with a simple GRU encoder while outperforming methods that use pretrained language models. Controlled experiments further confirm that the path-space penalty remains bounded during fine-tuning and that the CTMC generator adapts to shifted rewards faster than deterministic baselines. The candidate-set mechanism is supported by a stability analysis showing that the generator error decreases exponentially with candidate coverage.
core_methodology: The paper introduces DRIFT, an online fine-tuning method for offline-pretrained continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) policies in discrete action reinforcement learning. It uses an advantage-weighted discrete flow matching loss, path-space penalty, and candidate-set approximation to improve online performance while preserving offline knowledge. The candidate set is a subset of actions sampled from reference-policy rollouts and uniform exploration.
data_sources: The paper mentions 'prevailing discrete action RL task', but the exact data sources are not explicitly specified in the abstract. One example task listed is Jericho, which involves text-based games.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential comes from effectively leveraging offline data to initialize a policy that can then be fine-tuned online to adapt to changing market conditions or exploit transient opportunities in discrete trading actions. It could be applied to algorithmic order routing, options trading (selecting strike price/expiration), or portfolio rebalancing (discrete asset allocation choices). The ability to maintain knowledge learned offline and adapt to the online environment through path-space regularization strengthens its advantage in non-stationary markets.

title: A Family of Quaternion-Valued Differential Evolution Algorithms for Numerical Function Optimization
summary: The numerical optimization of continuous functions is a fundamental task in many scientific and engineering domains, ranging from mechanical design to training of artificial intelligence models. Among the most effective and widely used algorithms for this purpose is Differential Evolution (DE), known for its simplicity and strong performance. Recent research has shown that adapting AI models to operate over alternative number systems-such as complex numbers, quaternions, and geometric algebras-can improve model compactness and accuracy. However, such extensions remain underexplored in bio-inspired optimization algorithms. In particular, the use of quaternion algebra represents an emerging area in computational intelligence. This paper introduces a family of novel Quaternion-Valued Differential Evolution (QDE) algorithms that operate directly in the quaternion space. We propose several mutation strategies specifically designed to exploit the algebraic and geometric properties of quaternions. Results show that our QDE variants achieve faster convergence and superior performance on several function classes in the BBOB benchmark compared to the traditional real-valued DE algorithm.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Quaternion-Valued Differential Evolution (QDE) algorithms, which extend the traditional Differential Evolution optimization algorithm to operate in the quaternion space. It explores mutation strategies that leverage the algebraic and geometric properties of quaternions to improve convergence and performance in numerical function optimization. The study uses the BBOB benchmark to evaluate the proposed QDE variants.
data_sources: BBOB benchmark functions (not financial data).
alpha_potential: The potential alpha lies in using QDE for portfolio optimization or parameter tuning of existing trading algorithms. Standard optimization techniques can sometimes get stuck in local minima due to complex, high-dimensional parameter spaces. QDE's potentially faster convergence and superior performance could lead to better solutions and thus, improved trading performance. Specifically, optimizing risk models or hyperparameter tuning for ML models could be targeted.

title: Multi-Variable Conformal Prediction: Optimizing Prediction Sets without Data Splitting
summary: Conformal prediction constructs prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees, but its calibration stage is structurally constrained to a scalar score function and a single threshold variable - forcing shapes of prediction sets to be fixed before calibration, typically through data splitting. We introduce multi-variable conformal prediction (MCP), a framework that extends conformal prediction to vector-valued score functions with multiple simultaneous calibration variables. Building on scenario theory as a principled framework for certifying data-driven decisions, MCP unifies prediction set design and calibration into a single optimization problem, eliminating data splitting without sacrificing coverage guarantees. We propose two computationally efficient variants: RemMCP, grounded in constrained optimization with constraint removal, which admits a clean generalization of split conformal prediction; and RelMCP, based on iterative optimization with constraint relaxation, which supports non-convex score functions at the cost of possibly greater conservatism. Through numerical experiments on ellipsoidal and multi-modal prediction sets, we demonstrate that RemMCP and RelMCP consistently meet the target coverage with prediction set sizes smaller than or comparable to those of baselines with data split, while considerably reducing variance across calibration runs - a direct consequence of using all available data for shape optimization and calibration simultaneously.
core_methodology: The paper introduces Multi-Variable Conformal Prediction (MCP) which extends traditional conformal prediction by using vector-valued score functions and multiple calibration variables. This eliminates the need for data splitting in creating prediction sets with coverage guarantees. Two variants (RemMCP and RelMCP) offer computationally efficient implementations grounded in constrained optimization and iterative constraint relaxation respectively. The goal is to create smaller, more reliable prediction sets, reducing variance across calibrations.
data_sources: The paper mentions numerical experiments on ellipsoidal and multi-modal prediction sets, but does not specify financial datasets. Presumably, it can be used with any asset where you are trying to predict a range of possible future values.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in more accurate estimation of prediction intervals. Imagine using MCP to predict the range of possible returns of a stock, bond, or option. By creating smaller, better calibrated prediction sets, one can better assess risk. For example, one could utilize these tighter confidence intervals to construct more efficient portfolios, refine stop-loss strategies, or identify potentially mispriced securities where the current market price is significantly outside the prediction set. Furthermore, the elimination of data splitting can lead to more robust models, leveraging all available data for both shape optimization and calibration, especially relevant in regimes with limited historical data.

title: Online Learning-to-Defer with Varying Experts
summary: Learning-to-Defer (L2D) methods route each query either to a predictive model or to external experts. While existing work studies this problem in batch settings, real-world deployments require handling streaming data, changing expert availability, and shifting expert distribution. We introduce the first online L2D algorithm for multiclass classification with bandit feedback and a dynamically varying pool of experts. Our method achieves regret guarantees of $O((n+n_e)T^{2/3})$ in general and $O((n+n_e)\sqrt{T})$ under a low-noise condition, where $T$ is the time horizon, $n$ is the number of labels, and $n_e$ is the number of distinct experts observed across rounds. The analysis builds on novel $\mathcal{H}$-consistency bounds for the online framework, combined with first-order methods for online convex optimization. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach effectively extends standard Learning-to-Defer to settings with varying expert availability and reliability.
core_methodology: The paper proposes an online Learning-to-Defer (L2D) algorithm for multiclass classification in settings with streaming data, varying expert availability, and shifting expert distribution. It builds on $\mathcal{H}$-consistency bounds and online convex optimization with bandit feedback, adapting to dynamically changing expert pools and their reliability. The algorithm learns when to rely on its own internal model versus deferring to external 'experts' in a dynamic environment.
data_sources: The paper mentions experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. The abstract does not specify any particular financial data, so potential application is contingent on applicability to time-series data.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in its potential to improve prediction accuracy in situations where expert opinions (e.g., analyst ratings, sentiment indicators, macroeconomic forecasts) are used in conjunction with a base model. By dynamically learning the reliability of different experts and choosing when to defer to them, the algorithm could potentially filter out noise and improve overall forecast accuracy. This could lead to better trading decisions or risk management.

title: Autoregressive Learning in Joint KL: Sharp Oracle Bounds and Lower Bounds
summary: We study the fundamental and timely problem of learning long sequences in autoregressive modeling and next-token prediction under model misspecification, measured by the joint Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence. Our goal is to characterize how the sequence horizon \(H\) affects both approximation and estimation errors in this joint-distribution, sequence-level regime. By establishing matching upper and lower bounds, we provide, to our knowledge, the first complete characterization of long-horizon error behavior under the natural joint KL objective, with improved rates and optimality justification relative to existing work. On the approximation side, we show that joint KL admits a horizon-free approximation factor, in sharp contrast to Hellinger-based analyses that exhibit an \(Ω(H)\) dependence for computationally efficient methods; this isolates the choice of divergence as the source of approximation amplification. On the estimation side, we prove a fundamental information-theoretic lower bound of order \(Ω(H)\) that holds for both decomposable policy classes and fully shared policies, matching the \(\widetilde O(H)\) upper bounds achieved by computationally efficient algorithms. Our analysis clarifies the landscape of recent autoregressive learning results by aligning the log-loss training objective, the sequence-level evaluation metric, and the approximation metric {\color{black}through a sharp joint-KL oracle theory}. We further show that these joint-KL guarantees imply policy learning regret bounds at rates matching prior imitation learning literature.
core_methodology: The paper focuses on autoregressive modeling, specifically analyzing the joint Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence in the context of long sequence learning and next-token prediction. It establishes upper and lower bounds on error behavior, providing insights into approximation and estimation errors. The methodology centers on information-theoretic analysis and oracle inequalities to quantify the impact of sequence horizon on model misspecification. It clarifies the interplay between log-loss training, sequence-level evaluation, and approximation through a joint-KL framework, and links it to imitation learning regret bounds.
data_sources: The paper is primarily theoretical and does not directly specify particular dataset. However, the methodology it proposes is applicable to any time series data where autoregressive modeling and next-token prediction are relevant. This could include financial time series data such as stock prices, order book data, or macroeconomic indicators.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in improving the accuracy and efficiency of forecasting financial time series. By using insights of this paper, traders could potentially build more robust models that better handle model misspecification and long-range dependencies. This is particularly relevant in high-frequency trading or algorithmic execution where accurate short-term predictions are crucial. By reducing the forecasting error, a trader can potentially increase alpha generation. Also, the imitation learning aspect could be used for backtesting novel strategies that perform well on historical data.

title: Transferable Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning via Implicit Causal Graph Modeling
summary: Random delays weaken the temporal correspondence between actions and subsequent state feedback, making it difficult for agents to identify the true propagation process of action effects. In cross-task scenarios, changes in task objectives and reward formulations further reduce the reusability of previously acquired task knowledge. To address this problem, this paper proposes a transferable delay-aware reinforcement learning method based on implicit causal graph modeling. The proposed method uses a field-node encoder to represent high-dimensional observations as latent states with node-level semantics, and employs a message-passing mechanism to characterize dynamic causal dependencies among nodes, thereby learning transferable structured representations and environment dynamics knowledge. On this basis, imagination-driven behavior learning and planning are incorporated to optimize policies in the latent space, enabling cross-task knowledge transfer and rapid adaptation. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms baseline methods on DMC continuous control tasks with random delays. Cross-task transfer experiments further demonstrate that the learned structured representations and dynamics knowledge can be effectively transferred to new tasks and significantly accelerate policy adaptation.
core_methodology: This paper introduces a transferable delay-aware reinforcement learning (RL) method based on implicit causal graph modeling. It addresses the problem of random delays in state feedback and cross-task knowledge transfer limitation. It uses a field-node encoder to represent observations as latent states, employs a message-passing mechanism to model causal dependencies, and incorporates imagination-driven behavior learning and planning for policy optimization in the latent space.
data_sources: The paper focuses on DMC continuous control tasks, which are simulated environments. However, the methodology could be adapted to financial time series data.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential lies in its ability to model and adapt to delayed effects in market data. Many financial signals have delayed impacts, and this approach could improve trading strategy effectiveness by explicitly modeling these delays and transferring knowledge across different market regimes or assets. This is especially useful for modeling order book dynamics where actions/orders have lagged price impacts.
title_cn: 基于隐式因果图建模的可迁移延迟感知强化学习
summary_cn: 该论文提出了一种利用隐式因果图建模的延迟感知强化学习方法，可迁移应用于金融交易。该方法能有效处理市场数据中随机延迟造成的反馈滞后问题，并实现跨任务知识迁移，例如在不同市场环境或资产之间快速调整策略。潜在的应用包括优化考虑时间延迟的交易策略，特别是在订单簿动态建模中，其中订单行为具有滞后的价格影响。

title: In-context learning to predict critical transitions in dynamical systems
summary: Critical transitions - abrupt, often irreversible changes in system dynamics - arise across human and natural systems, often with catastrophic consequences. Real-world observations of such shifts remain scarce, preventing the development of reliable early warning systems. Conventional statistical and spectral indicators, such as increasing variance, tend to fail under realistic conditions of limited data and correlated noise, whereas existing deep learning classifiers do not extrapolate beyond their training data distribution. In this work, we introduce TipPFN, an in-context learning (ICL) framework that uses a prior-data fitted network to infer a system's proximity to a critical transition. Trained on our novel synthetic data generator, which is based on canonical bifurcation scenarios coupled to diverse, randomized stochastic dynamics, TipPFN flexibly capitalizes on contexts of various sizes, complexity and dimensionalities. We demonstrate robust, state-of-the-art early detection of critical transitions in previously unseen tipping regimes, sim-to-real examples, and real-world observations in both ICL and zero-shot settings.
core_methodology: The paper introduces TipPFN, an in-context learning (ICL) framework using a prior-data fitted network to predict critical transitions in dynamical systems. The network is trained on synthetic data generated from canonical bifurcation scenarios coupled with randomized stochastic dynamics. ICL allows adaptation to new or unseen data without retraining.
data_sources: Primarily synthetic data generated from canonical bifurcation scenarios. It also mentions sim-to-real examples and real-world observations, but these are not explicitly listed data sources.
alpha_potential: The potential lies in identifying and capitalizing on market regime shifts or impending market crashes before they occur. Predicting critical transitions could provide early warning signals for significant price changes, allowing for preemptive trading strategies to mitigate risk or profit from the shift. This can be applied to broader macroeconomic indicators as well if they show similar transition dynamics.

title: Missingness-MDPs: Bridging the Theory of Missing Data and POMDPs
summary: We introduce missingness-MDPs (miss-MDPs), a novel subclass of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) that incorporates the theory of missing data. A miss-MDP is a POMDP whose observation function is a missingness function, specifying the probability that individual state features are missing (i.e., unobserved) at a time step. The literature distinguishes three canonical missingness types: missing (1) completely at random (MCAR), (2) at random (MAR), and (3) not at random (MNAR). Our planning problem is to compute near-optimal policies for a miss-MDP with an unknown missingness function, given a dataset of action-observation trajectories. Achieving such optimality guarantees for policies requires learning the missingness function from data, which is infeasible for general POMDPs. To overcome this challenge, we exploit the structural properties of different missingness types to derive probably approximately correct (PAC) algorithms for learning the missingness function. These algorithms yield an approximate but fully specified miss-MDP that we solve using off-the-shelf planning methods. We prove that, with high probability, the resulting policies are epsilon-optimal in the true miss-MDP. Empirical results confirm the theory and demonstrate superior performance of our approach over two model-free POMDP methods.
core_methodology: The paper introduces 'missingness-MDPs' (miss-MDPs), a subclass of POMDPs dealing with missing data. It focuses on learning the missingness function (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) from action-observation trajectories to create an approximate but fully specified MDP. This is achieved using PAC algorithms and off-the-shelf planning methods to derive near-optimal policies.
data_sources: The paper uses datasets of action-observation trajectories, although the specific type of data is not explicitly mentioned. In a financial context, this could refer to historical market data (price, volume, order book) or alternative data sources where data points are often missing or incomplete.
alpha_potential: The alpha potential arises from the improved handling of missing data in financial time series. Many financial datasets suffer from missing values or irregular sampling. By explicitly modeling the missingness mechanism, the miss-MDPs could lead to more robust state estimation and better trading decisions than methods that ignore missingness or use simple imputation techniques. The model's ability to determine if the data is MCAR, MAR, or MNAR can lead to exploiting market behavior driven from biased sets of observed data.

title: Delay-Empowered Causal Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
summary: Many real-world tasks involve delayed effects, where the outcomes of actions emerge after varying time lags. Existing delay-aware reinforcement learning methods often rely on state augmentation, prior knowledge of delay distributions, or access to non-delayed data, limiting their generalization. Hierarchical reinforcement learning, by contrast, inherently offers advantages in handling delays due to its hierarchical structure, yet existing methods are restricted to fixed delays. To address these limitations, we propose Delay-Empowered Causal Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (DECHRL). DECHRL explicitly models both the causal structure of state transitions and their associated stochastic delay distributions. These are then incorporated into a delay-aware empowerment objective that drives proactive exploration toward highly controllable states, thereby improving performance under temporal uncertainty. We evaluate DECHRL in modified 2D-Minecraft and MiniGrid environments featuring stochastic delays. Experimental results show that DECHRL effectively models temporal delays and significantly outperforms baselines in decision-making under temporal uncertainty.
core_methodology: Delay-Empowered Causal Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (DECHRL). It models causal relationships and their associated stochastic delay distributions. An empowerment objective fosters proactive exploration toward controllable states, mitigating temporal uncertainty.
data_sources: Evaluated in modified 2D-Minecraft and MiniGrid environments, implying potentially applicable to simulated market environments or order book simulations.
alpha_potential: The potential lies in capturing delayed effects in markets, such as news sentiment impact that unfolds over time, order execution delays, or the lagged effects of macroeconomic news. This could be applied to modeling market microstructure dynamics or predicting delayed price reactions.

title: Optimal Policy Learning under Budget and Coverage Constraints
summary: We study optimal policy learning under combined budget and minimum coverage constraints. We show that the problem admits a knapsack-type structure and that the optimal policy can be characterized by an affine threshold rule involving both budget and coverage shadow prices. We establish that the linear programming relaxation of the combinatorial solution has an O(1) integrality gap, implying asymptotic equivalence with the optimal discrete allocation. Building on this result, we analyze two implementable approaches: a Greedy-Lagrangian (GLC) and a rank-and-cut (RC) algorithm. We show that the GLC closely approximates the optimal solution and achieves near-optimal performance in finite samples. By contrast, RC is approximately optimal whenever the coverage constraint is slack or costs are homogeneous, while misallocation arises only when cost heterogeneity interacts with a binding coverage constraint. Monte Carlo evidence supports these findings.
core_methodology: The paper presents an approach to optimal policy learning under budget and coverage constraints, framed as a knapsack problem solvable with a linear programming relaxation. Two algorithms, Greedy-Lagrangian (GLC) and rank-and-cut (RC), are proposed to approximate the optimal discrete allocation. The optimal policy follows an affine threshold rule based on budget and coverage shadow prices.
data_sources: The abstract suggests using Monte Carlo simulations. Applying this in practice to financial markets would likely involve backtesting on historical financial data such as order book data or stock price data.
alpha_potential: The 'optimal policy learning' suggests a potential for dynamic asset allocation or order execution strategies. The budget constraint could represent risk limits, while the coverage constraint may represent exposure to certain sectors or factors. The algorithms could be used to efficiently allocate capital across assets subject to these constraints, potentially leading to better risk-adjusted returns. The affine threshold rule could be used as a signal to trigger trades based on the budget and coverage shadow prices.
